target_customer: Hospital pathology labs and research institutions that need fast digital images of fresh tissue
problem: Conventional pathology cuts, fixes and stains tissue, which takes time and consumes the sample. Frozen section takes about twenty minutes, destroys part of the sample and needs a pathologist on site.
business_model: Medical device sales of an imaging system for fresh tissue, with grant funding in early years

founders.name: Mei Wang
founders.background_notes: YC page gives no bio. A Tulane page seen only in search results describes the startup as spun out of Tulane doctoral students.

founders.name: Quincy Brown
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page; no bio.

founders.name: David Tulman
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page; no bio.

technical_complexity.rationale: Fresh-tissue fluorescence imaging with high contrast and no sample loss requires optics, instrument engineering and regulatory work. Hardware plus medical device registration for a six person team.

defensibility.rationale: Device hardware, imaging method and registration as a medical device raise barriers, but large pathology vendors could respond.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No source shows incumbents copying or buying the approach. Several vendors now sell rapid frozen section scanning, which is a different workflow.

market_need_then: Pathology is a slow bottleneck in cancer surgery and diagnosis, and NSF funded the project in 2018 on that need. Direct demand evidence from customers was not found.

branding.domain_note: Website at instapathbio.com, not an exact .com for the name.

identity.voice_and_tone: Short and workflow focused: Fresh tissue. Digital in minutes.

branding.brand_signature: Tagline Fresh tissue. Digital in minutes.
branding.community_and_virality: Won a Tulane business competition and a $30,000 International Business Model Competition grand prize per search summaries; no consumer community.

brand_strength.rationale: A coined name combining instant and pathology. Press about the brand is limited to competition wins and a pending trademark.

outcome_analysis: Instapath is active and small, funded mainly by NSF grants and registered a Class I device in 2024 according to a directory citing a March 2025 Tulane interview. No equity round was found and database totals range from about $1.7M to $6M. The company is still in early commercialization, so it is neither a success nor a failure yet.
notes: Competitor list is empty because the searches found only 2024 to 2026 vendor pages, not sources dated near the 2019 batch. Funding totals conflict across databases (Persana $1.7M, PitchBook $2.11M, CB Insights $3.16M, Caplight $6.14M). The 2021 grant is from the Grantome aggregator and the 2018 grant from one local news outlet. A Caplight banner about a $16M Series A appeared to belong to another company and is ignored. The device is called Nova on the company site and Neo in a 2025 interview. Company site calls Nova an FDA Class I device.
